idiom_name: QObject + Q_PROPERTY(NOTIFY) + signals/slots, bound from QML or widgets
implementation_notes: The canonical C++ presentation model is a QObject whose screen fields are Q_PROPERTYs with NOTIFY signals: the view declares bindings (a QML property binding) or connects slots, and reads the model's derived properties, while writes go through the setters that emit notify. The model contains no widget types, so it can be constructed and exercised in a plain test; the binding is the synchronization. Choose this form when Qt is already the toolkit; the Qt 6 bindable-property variant buys automatic dependency tracking, and the framework-free variant is the fallback for non-Qt code.
pitfalls: Q_PROPERTY notifications are emitted by the WRITE accessor: writing the member directly (or using MEMBER without NOTIFY) leaves QML bindings and connected slots stale - the Qt property documentation requires NOTIFY to be emitted whenever the value really changes.
The meta-object compiler must see the class; a missing moc step appears as undefined vtable references rather than a compile error.

Qt removes connections when sender or receiver is destroyed, but the signals/slots documentation warns that function-pointer connections can still deliver a signal during the destructor window after a derived class has been destroyed - disconnect explicitly in destructors where that matters.

variants.name: Qt 6 bindable properties with dependency-tracked binding expressions
variants.implementation_notes: Qt 6 adds bindable properties: a Q_PROPERTY with the BINDABLE attribute is backed by a QProperty<T> or QObjectBindableProperty, and QBindable::setBinding installs a binding expression that is re-evaluated whenever any bindable dependency changes; QML binds to the same property. The model keeps its state and decisions, but the synchronization is expressed as declarative bindings instead of notify handlers. The documented rules matter here: getters and setters must be trivial, every dependency must itself be bindable (changes to non-bindable properties are silently ignored), binding expressions must not read or write the property they define, and the system is not thread-safe.
pitfalls: Bindable properties are not thread-safe: the documentation states a bindable property must not be read or modified by any thread other than the one it was created in, and an object owning or feeding a binding must not be moved between threads.
Binding expressions may evaluate several times and must not read or write the property they define - a self-referential binding is an evaluation loop.
Writing intermediate or transient values to a bindable property notifies dependents on every write, exposing half-updated state; compute into a local and assign once.

variants.name: Framework-free model with std::function observer list
variants.implementation_notes: Without a toolkit the model is a plain class and the synchronization is a list of std::function<void()> observers that the view registers; after each mutation the model notifies, and the view re-reads the properties it needs. This keeps the model toolkit-free and testable at the cost of hand-written plumbing; it is the fallback when one core must serve several toolkits or when no UI framework is available.
pitfalls: A callback that captures the view by reference dangles if the view is destroyed before the model; lifetime and unsubscription are the caller's responsibility.
Notifying while iterating the subscriber list breaks if a callback subscribes or unsubscribes: iterate over a copy.
std::function copies the callable, so a captured reference is not a weak reference - it keeps the referent alive.
